tier_reason: First-party one-sentence claim ('faster 2-3 times than C++ std::string::find') in strstr/README.rst; the harness (strstr/test.cpp, analyze.py, Makefile with g++ -O3) is public but no results, CPU model or compiler version are stored, so it falls short of A and has no independent measurement for B.

corrections.workload: test64 times libc strstr, std::string::find and the 64-bit SWAR first/last-byte filter (10 iterations each, gettimeofday) for every unique word extracted from i386.txt by make_words.sh, so each search succeeds at the word's first occurrence in the same text; analyze.py then prints a histogram of per-word speed-ratio buckets (slower, same, 2-2.99x, 3-3.99x, ... faster) against std::string::find and against libc strstr.
corrections.caveats: The 2-3x figure is a single README sentence matching analyze.py's '2.00 - 2.99 faster' bucket; no stored output, CPU, compiler version or libstdc++/glibc version, so it cannot be checked without running (the Makefile wgets i386.txt from an MIT course URL). The harness also times libc strstr (analyze.py and the README mislabel it 'strlen'), but no margin over strstr is claimed; strstr must also scan for the terminator while the SWAR routine gets the length. Timing is 10 iterations with microsecond gettimeofday and no warm-up, and words are taken from the searched text, so many searches end early and are timer-resolution noise. By code reading (not run), strstr64.cpp has correctness bugs: the SWAR zero-byte test can flag the byte above a real candidate through borrow, and memcmp checks only needle[1..k-1], so needle 'abb' in text 'a`bb' returns 1 instead of not-found; the loop 'i < n - k' with step 8 skips the last start position when n-k is a multiple of 8; and the 8-byte loads read up to 5 bytes past the string terminator. verify.cpp checks only words from the same text, so these cases are not exercised. The linked article 0x80.pl/articles/simd-friendly-karp-rabin.html was unreachable (DNS ENOTFOUND). last_commit is the last commit touching strstr/ (2016-01-17); the toys repo itself was last pushed 2026-04-08. Shares its repo URL with the avx512-string entry, which needs separate ids at merge time.

notes: Claim and harness verified on github.com and raw files; tier C stands. Shortcomings for the orchestrator: single-sentence first-party claim with no stored results or CPU; noisy 10-iteration gettimeofday timing; code-reading correctness bugs in strstr64 (borrow false positive with unchecked first byte, skipped last position, over-read) that rarely trigger on the word-list workload.

tier_reason: The Overview.md table matches every quoted number (memory.copy intrinsic vs the Emscripten i32 loop and hand-unrolled i32/i64 loops); it is the proposal author's own run with the benchmark in a public gist, but the CPU model, V8 version and flags are not stated and the intrinsic needs the author's unpublished V8 hack, so C.

corrections.caveats: Baseline is a 2017-era Emscripten wasm memcpy (gist c57dc945, memcpy.wast: byte prologue to 4-byte alignment, i32.load/i32.store word loop, byte tail; byte path when src and dst alignments differ) plus hand-unrolled variants, not a native libc memcpy; the prototype memory.copy simply called V8's native MemMove, so this is native memmove versus wasm-compiled loops. The benchmark gist (b8e8bc0c, memcpy.js, created 2017-10-26) is public, but its data initialisation and verification block is commented out, and the 'intrinsic' module's exported _memcpy body is a stub returning 0 that only the author's hacked V8 replaced with memory.copy, so the intrinsic column cannot be reproduced on a stock engine from the gist; the size-dependent curve (1.382 Gib/s at 32 B rising to 29.994 at 512 KiB, falling to 11.760 at 1 MiB) is consistent with real copying, not a no-op. Engine version, CPU model and flags are not given, and the stated 'L3 256k' looks mis-stated. Single first-party run. The repository is archived (2021-11-03); WebAssembly/proposals finished-proposals.md lists Bulk memory operations as finished and merged into core spec 2.0 (WG 2021-02-10), so memory.copy is now a standard instruction implemented by engines rather than a library.
corrections.license: Per-directory (repo LICENSE): document/ W3C Software and Document Notice and License; interpreter/ and test/ Apache-2.0; papers/ CC-BY-4.0
corrections.stars_or_usage: 82 stars, 21 forks; archived Nov 3 2021; finished proposal merged into WebAssembly core spec 2.0 per WebAssembly/proposals finished-proposals.md

notes: Numbers verified exactly against Overview.md; tier C stands, usability stays reference (an engine instruction, not copyable library code). Shortcomings: off-baseline (wasm loops, not native libc), benchmark gist has verification commented out and needs an unpublished V8 hack for the intrinsic column, no CPU model or engine version. maintenance_status set to finished because the WebAssembly CG lists the proposal as finished and archived the repo after merge; revert to abandoned if archived-means-abandoned is preferred.

tier_reason: Neither README nor the string README gives any number; string/bench/memcpy.c benchmarks libc memcpy beside __memcpy_aarch64/_simd/_sve/_mops/__memcpy_arm but no results are published, and the commit messages opened quote only gains over earlier versions of the same routine (9190f2f: random memset benchmark 24% faster on Neoverse N1), not over a libc.

corrections.baseline: System libc string.h routines; string/bench/memcpy.c runs the libc memcpy alongside the Arm variants with SPEC2017-derived size and alignment distributions, but no libc (glibc, musl, newlib, bionic) is named and no results are published
corrections.stars_or_usage: 716 stars, 126 forks; vendored in FreeBSD as contrib/arm-optimized-routines (README says v25.01); newlib syncs its aarch64 memchr, memcpy and strchr from it (WebSearch snippet only); biannual releases, latest v26.07
corrections.caveats: Tier D: no performance numbers versus any libc in the repo pages opened; string/bench/{memcpy,memset,strlen}.c are harnesses without stored results, and commit messages report only gains over the routine's previous version (e.g. 9190f2f, 24% on a random memset benchmark on Neoverse N1; 375f32e says the SVE2 strlen beats the AdvSIMD versions, no numbers). The same maintainers upstream AArch64 string routines to glibc, so against a current glibc on AArch64 the gap may be small; the expected win is over generic C libc code (musl, newlib generic) and older libcs, which is not measured here. AArch64 and 32-bit Arm only. The newlib usage comes from a search snippet because sourceware.org was unreachable. The same repo also holds math, fp and networking subprojects that other categories may report separately.

notes: Kept at D and not rejected as not-notable: under 1k stars but widely used (FreeBSD vendors it in contrib/, newlib syncs from it per snippet). Shortcomings: no published numbers versus any libc; harness exists (string/bench) but results are not stored; gains likely small versus glibc AArch64, which shares authors and code lineage.
